## What the timeline cache holds
For each active user, a list of post ids (and maybe a small score or author id) in reverse chronological order, kept in memory, such as a Redis list or sorted set keyed by user id.
```
timeline:{userId} -> [postId, postId, ...]   (capped, e.g. 800)
```
- Storing ids only keeps memory small: 800 ids at 8 bytes is about 6.4 KB per user. For 100M active users that is on the order of 640 GB before overhead, spread across a sharded cache cluster, which is feasible.
- Hydration: a read gets the ids, then multi-gets post bodies from a post cache, author profiles from a user cache, and counters (likes) from a counter store. Each is a separate cache with its own hit-rate target.
- Cache misses: for users not in cache (inactive), rebuild by pulling from followed accounts, then store.
- TTL or LRU eviction keeps only active users resident.
- Pagination uses a cursor (last post id or score) rather than offset, so newly inserted posts do not shift pages.

## Keeping it consistent
- New post: fan-out workers LPUSH then LTRIM to the cap.
- Delete: filter at read time against a deleted-posts check. Lazy cleanup avoids touching millions of lists.
- Follow or unfollow: backfill or filter lazily.
- Eventual consistency is acceptable: a post appearing a few seconds late is fine.

## Ranking
Pure chronological order is simple, but engagement ranking increases usefulness.
- Candidate generation: take the timeline entries plus pulled celebrity posts plus recommendations, a few hundred candidates.
- Features: post age, author affinity (how often the viewer interacts with the author), post engagement (likes, comments, shares), media type, and negative signals (hidden, muted).
- Scoring: a lightweight model (logistic regression or gradient-boosted trees, then neural models at scale) predicts the probability of engagement. Sort by predicted score.
- Keep a latency budget of tens to a few hundred ms for the whole request, so heavy models run on a shortlist, in stages (cheap first-pass, expensive re-rank).
- Post-processing: diversify (not ten posts from one author), dedupe, apply policy and safety filters, insert ads at slots.
- Features are precomputed and stored in a feature store, with offline training and online serving.

## Trade-offs
- Ranking makes cached order unstable: refreshing a feed can reorder. Often the ranked page is snapshotted for the session, so scrolling is stable.
- Cold-start users and new posts need exploration slots.
- Measure with online experiments (A/B), as offline metrics can mislead.

## Follow-up
How do you serve 1M reads per second? Shard cache by user id, replicate hot shards, add local in-process caches for hot posts, and use a CDN for media.
keyPoints: Timeline cache stores capped lists of post ids per active user; content is hydrated from separate post, user and counter caches.
Use cursor pagination, lazy handling of deletes and eventual consistency for follow and unfollow.
Ranking is staged: candidate generation, feature fetch, cheap then heavy scoring, then diversity and policy filters within a tight latency budget.
Evict inactive users and rebuild their timelines on demand by pull.

## Why WebSockets
HTTP request/response is client-initiated. Chat, live updates and presence need the server to push. A WebSocket (RFC 6455) starts as an HTTP request that upgrades to a persistent, full-duplex TCP connection. After the handshake, either side can send small frames with very low overhead. Alternatives: long polling (simple, more overhead), Server-Sent Events (server to client only, auto-reconnect), and for mobile, platform push as a fallback when the app is closed.

## The stateful gateway problem
A WebSocket lives on one specific server for its lifetime. A single server can hold a large number of mostly idle connections: tens to a few hundred thousand with tuning (file descriptors, kernel buffers, memory per connection of a few KB to tens of KB). So 10M concurrent users needs on the order of 50 to 200 gateway servers.
- Connection servers are stateful, unlike ordinary web servers. Put them behind a layer-4 or layer-7 load balancer that supports WebSocket upgrades. Use least-connections balancing.
- Keep gateways dumb: they authenticate, hold the socket, and relay. Business logic lives in stateless backend services.
- Deploys and scale-in drain connections gradually. Clients reconnect with exponential backoff and jitter. A deploy or crash that drops 100k connections at once causes a reconnect storm, so jitter matters.
- Heartbeats (ping/pong every 20 to 30 s) detect dead connections and keep NAT and proxy idle timeouts from closing them.

## Connection registry
To send user B a message, the backend must know which gateway holds B's socket.
```
conn:{userId} -> {gatewayId, connectionId, lastSeen}   (Redis, with TTL)
```
- On connect, the gateway writes the mapping (a user can have several devices, so store a set per user). On disconnect or heartbeat timeout, it removes it. A TTL refreshed by heartbeats cleans up crashed gateways.
- Sending: the chat service looks up the registry, then sends to that gateway (via internal RPC) or publishes to a channel the gateway subscribes to (Redis pub/sub, Kafka, NATS) like gw:{gatewayId}. The gateway writes to the socket.
- If the user is offline (no registry entry), persist the message and fire a mobile push notification.
- Group chat: the message service resolves members, and fans out to each member's gateway. Large groups and channels might use per-channel pub/sub with gateways subscribing on behalf of connected members.

## Pitfalls
- Registry staleness: the message goes to a gateway that no longer has the socket. Treat delivery as unreliable and rely on acks and sync on reconnect, not on the registry being perfect.
- Sticky routing is unnecessary for the gateway layer if the registry is used.
- Auth: validate tokens at connect and on a refresh schedule.
- Backpressure: a slow client must not make the gateway buffer unlimited data. Use bounded send queues and drop or disconnect.
keyPoints: WebSockets give a persistent full-duplex channel; gateways are stateful and hold hundreds of thousands of idle connections each.
A connection registry (user to gateway id, with TTL refreshed by heartbeats) lets backend services route a message to the right gateway.
Handle reconnect storms with backoff and jitter, graceful draining on deploys, and heartbeats for dead connections.
If the user is offline, store the message and send a push notification; do not trust the registry as the delivery guarantee.

## Ordering
Messages in a conversation must appear in the same order for everyone. Clocks on clients and servers disagree, so wall-clock timestamps are not enough.
- Per-conversation sequence number: the server assigns a monotonically increasing number per conversation (or per user inbox) when it accepts the message. Clients sort by it. Generate with a per-conversation counter (an atomic increment in Redis or a database row), or partition the message log by conversation id so a single partition leader orders messages (Kafka with key = conversationId).
- Time-sortable ids (Snowflake style: timestamp bits, machine id, sequence) work for per-shard ordering, but cross-machine order is only approximate.
- Client-generated ids: the client attaches a unique message id (UUID) so retries are idempotent (the server dedups) and the UI can show the message optimistically before it is confirmed.
- Ordering is only needed within a conversation, which makes sharding by conversation id natural and keeps the counter off the global path.

## Delivery and read receipts
States: sent (server stored it), delivered (reached the recipient device), read (recipient viewed it).
- Sender gets an ack from the server once the message is persisted (the single tick).
- When the recipient device receives it, it sends a delivery ack back, and the server updates the state and notifies the sender (double tick).
- When the recipient opens the chat, the client sends a read receipt, usually as "read up to sequence N", not one per message, which cuts traffic.
- Receipts are small events that travel the same route in reverse. In large groups, receipts are often aggregated or dropped, since per-member receipts for a 10k group are too much.
- Delivery is at-least-once: the sender retries until acked, and the server dedups by message id.

## Offline sync
A device that was offline must catch up on reconnect without gaps or duplicates.
- Messages are stored durably per conversation (and a per-user inbox or sync log). Persist before acking the sender.
- The client remembers the last sequence it has per conversation (or one global sync cursor). On reconnect it asks "give me everything after cursor X" and the server returns the missing range, paged.
- Detect gaps: if the live stream delivers sequence 12 when the client has 10, it fetches 11 from the server instead of showing a hole.
- Push notifications (APNs and FCM) wake the app when it is closed, carrying minimal data. The app then syncs.
- Multiple devices: each device keeps its own cursor. The server stores the log once, per user.
- Retention and local storage: the client stores history in a local database (SQLite) so it displays instantly, then syncs the delta. Older history loads on scroll.
- End-to-end encrypted systems keep messages queued on the server until delivered, and deliver ciphertext only.

## Pitfalls
- Using timestamps for ordering (clock skew).
- Treating the push channel as reliable. It is a hint only, and the sync API is the source of truth.
- Sequence counter becoming a hotspot for huge group chats: shard channels, or accept fan-in on one partition since message rates per conversation are modest.
keyPoints: Order messages with a server-assigned per-conversation sequence number, not client or wall-clock timestamps.
Client-generated message ids make retries idempotent and allow optimistic UI.
Receipts progress sent, delivered, read; read receipts use read-up-to-N and are aggregated in large groups.
Offline sync: durable log, client cursor, fetch everything after the cursor, detect gaps; push notifications are only wake-up hints.

hld-feed-chat:4.body:
## What presence is
Showing whether a user is online, offline or away (and "last seen"). It looks small but has a large fan-out: every status change must reach everyone watching that user, and status changes are frequent.

## Detecting online status
- Heartbeats: while the client holds a WebSocket, it sends a ping every 5 to 30 s. The server records last_seen in a store with a TTL of a few heartbeats, for example Redis: SET presence:{userId} online EX 30. If the key expires, the user is offline.
- Connection events alone are not reliable: network drops often do not close the TCP connection cleanly, so heartbeat timeout is the real detector.
- Flapping: a user going through a tunnel or switching networks disconnects and reconnects. Apply a grace period (wait 10 to 30 s before announcing offline) to avoid spamming status changes.
- Multiple devices: online if any device is connected. Track per device and aggregate.
- Away or idle: derived from client activity reports.

## Publishing changes: fan-out
Alice's status should reach her friends who are currently online and looking.
- Pub/sub per user: friends' gateways subscribe to channel presence:{aliceId} for the users visible on the friend's screen. On a change, publish once and subscribers receive it.
- For small friend lists (hundreds), push to online friends directly. For huge audiences (celebrities, big channels), do not push at all. Instead, fetch presence on demand when the viewer opens the profile or visible list, or poll at low frequency, since pushing is too expensive.
- Fetch on demand, then subscribe only to what is visible on screen (the contact list page, the open chat) and unsubscribe on leaving.
- Batch and rate limit updates (coalesce within a second).

## Numbers
100M online users, each changing state perhaps a few times a day, plus heartbeats. Heartbeats at 1 per 20 s from 100M users are 5M writes per second, which is large. Reduce by writing to the store less often than clients ping: gateways keep a local view and refresh the Redis TTL every minute, or refresh only when the TTL is nearly gone.

## Storage
- Redis for current presence (ephemeral, a loss only briefly shows wrong status). Last-seen timestamp in a durable store if the product shows it, written on disconnect rather than every heartbeat.
- Shard by user id.

## Trade-offs and privacy
- Accuracy versus cost: seconds of staleness is acceptable.
- Privacy controls: hide last seen, appear offline. Enforce on the server, not just the client.

## Pitfall
Naive design, where every status change fans out to all friends, makes load proportional to friends count times changes, which blows up for users with large friend lists.
keyPoints: Detect presence by heartbeats with TTL in Redis, not by connection close events; use a grace period for flapping.
A user is online if any device is connected; aggregate per device state.
Fan out status only to interested online viewers via per-user pub/sub; for huge audiences fetch on demand instead of pushing.
Cut heartbeat write load by refreshing the store less often than clients ping, and subscribe only to visible contacts.

## Timeouts
A call without a timeout can hang forever and tie up a thread, connection and memory in the caller, so the caller fails because the callee is slow. Rules:
- Every remote call has a timeout: connect, request and overall deadline.
- Choose from data: set it near the callee's high percentile (for example a bit above p99.9) so you cut off the long tail without causing spurious failures. The AWS Builders' Library suggests picking an acceptable false-timeout rate and reading the latency at that percentile.
- Propagate deadlines: if the user-facing budget is 500 ms and 200 ms is spent, pass 300 ms downstream. Downstream stops working on abandoned requests.
- Timeouts must shrink as you go deeper, not grow, or the caller gives up before the callee finishes.

## Retries
Retries fix transient failures (a dropped packet, a restarting node), but they are dangerous when the failure is overload.
- Retry only idempotent operations, or ones protected by an idempotency key. A retried "charge card" without a key can double charge.
- Retry only retryable errors: timeouts, connection resets, 503, 429. Not 400s.
- Limit attempts (2 or 3) and total time.
- Retry amplification: with retries at each of 3 layers and 3 attempts each, the bottom service sees up to 27 times the load at the worst moment, exactly when it is struggling (a retry storm that prevents recovery). Retry at one layer only, and use a retry budget (for example retries allowed at most 10 percent of the request volume) or token bucket that stops retrying when the failure rate is high. gRPC and Envoy both support budgets or limits.
- Combine with a circuit breaker so retries stop when the dependency is clearly down.

## Exponential backoff
Wait longer after each failure: delay = min(cap, base * 2^attempt). For example 100 ms, 200 ms, 400 ms, 800 ms, capped at 20 s. This gives the dependency room to recover, and spreads load over time.

## Jitter
Without randomness, clients that failed together retry together, creating synchronised waves (thundering herd). Jitter spreads them.
- Full jitter: sleep = random(0, min(cap, base * 2^attempt)). The AWS Architecture Blog showed this reduces total calls and completion time compared with no jitter.
- Equal jitter: half fixed, half random. Decorrelated jitter: sleep = min(cap, random(base, previous_sleep * 3)).
```
for attempt in 0..max:
    try call(timeout=remaining_deadline); return
    sleep(random(0, min(cap, base * 2**attempt)))
```
Add jitter to periodic jobs and cache expiry (TTL plus random) too, to avoid synchronised spikes.

## Interview points
Tie them together: deadline budget, bounded retries on one layer, backoff with full jitter, idempotency keys for writes, a circuit breaker, and metrics on retry rate.

Retry only idempotent operations on transient errors, bounded, at a single layer; use retry budgets to prevent amplification.
Exponential backoff spaces retries; jitter (full jitter is a good default) breaks synchronised thundering herds.
Nested retries multiply load (3 layers x 3 attempts = 27x), so combine with circuit breakers.

## Hedged requests (tail latency)
At scale, the slowest of many parallel calls dominates user latency. If a request fans out to 100 backends and each has a 1 percent chance of being slow, about 63 percent of user requests hit at least one slow call. Slowness is often random (garbage collection, noisy neighbour, a disk hiccup), not a systematic property of a request.

Hedging: send the request to one replica, and if no response arrives within a short delay, send a duplicate to another replica. Use whichever answers first and cancel the other.
- Set the hedge delay near the p95 latency of the service, so only about 5 percent of requests are duplicated. Google's "The Tail at Scale" paper reported large p99.9 reductions for a small increase in load with this approach.
- Only for idempotent, read-like operations, since the work may run twice.
- Tied requests: send to two replicas at once and each tells the other when it starts, so the loser cancels, reducing wasted work.
- Do not hedge when the system is overloaded: it adds load. Combine with a budget, and disable under high load.
- Needs spare capacity and independent replicas (different failure domains).

## Load shedding
When demand exceeds capacity, accepting everything makes every request slow, queues grow, latency exceeds client timeouts, and useful throughput (goodput) collapses, since work is done for clients who already gave up. Load shedding deliberately rejects excess work early so the accepted work succeeds.
- Fail fast: return 503 or 429 quickly, cheaply, with Retry-After. Do the check at the edge before expensive work.
- Triggers: concurrency limit exceeded, queue wait above a threshold, CPU saturation, or request age (drop requests already older than the client's deadline).
- Prioritise: shed by criticality. Keep health checks, logins and payments. Drop prefetching, analytics and batch work first. Per-tenant quotas stop one client from consuming all capacity.
- Adaptive concurrency limits (AIMD, as in Netflix's concurrency-limits library) find a safe limit automatically.
- Bounded queues, preferably LIFO under overload so the freshest request, most likely to still be useful, is served first.
- Tune clients to not retry instantly on 503, or shedding turns into a retry storm.

## Example
A search service sized for 10k QPS receives 15k. Without shedding every request takes 5 s and times out. With a concurrency limit it serves 10k within normal latency, and rejects 5k immediately. Rejected clients back off, and autoscaling adds capacity.

## Pitfalls
Shedding based on CPU alone is laggy. Hedging plus retries plus overload becomes a self-inflicted outage. Measure the hedge rate and shed rate as metrics.
keyPoints: Hedged requests duplicate slow idempotent calls after about p95 latency to cut tail latency at the cost of a few percent extra load.
Never hedge or retry blindly during overload: budget it and disable under high load.
Load shedding rejects excess work early with 503 or 429 so accepted requests meet latency, protecting goodput.
Shed by priority and tenant, drop requests already past the client's deadline, and prefer LIFO queues under overload.

## Graceful degradation
When a dependency fails or load spikes, serve a reduced but useful experience instead of an error page. Decide in advance which features are essential (checkout) and which are optional (recommendations, reviews, personalisation).

Techniques:
- Fallback to a default: if the recommendation service times out, show popular items from a cache or a static list.
- Serve stale: return cached data past its TTL when the origin is down (stale-if-error). A slightly old product price list is better than an outage, but be careful with data that must be exact, such as balances and stock at purchase time.
- Disable non-critical features: feature flags or automatic switches turn off heavy functionality (search suggestions, live counters) when under stress.
- Reduce quality: lower image resolution, skip personalisation, return fewer results, shorten page size.
- Read-only mode: if the primary database is down, allow browsing while rejecting writes, with a clear message.
- Queue and defer: accept the write into a durable queue and process later ("we got your order, confirmation by email").
- Partial responses: a page assembled from many services renders what it can and hides failed widgets, each fetch with its own timeout.
- Be careful with fallbacks: they are rarely exercised, and can fail in surprising ways or create a second bug under load. The AWS Builders' Library warns against fallback code paths that only run during failures. Prefer fail-fast with static stability, or test fallbacks regularly.

## Bulkheads
Isolate resources so a failure in one area cannot drain shared resources, like watertight ship compartments.
- Separate thread pools, connection pools or semaphores per downstream dependency. If the reviews service hangs, only its pool is exhausted.
- Separate instance groups or clusters for critical and non-critical traffic (checkout versus catalog browse), or for large customers versus small.
- Per-tenant quotas and rate limits, plus shuffle sharding: assign each customer to a small random subset of cells, so a poison customer only affects the few others that share exactly the same subset.
- Cell-based architecture: the system is split into independent cells, each serving a slice of users, so a failure or bad deploy is bounded to one cell.
- Cost: lower utilisation efficiency, since reserved capacity may idle, and more config to manage.

## Example
Product page calls catalog, price, reviews and recommendations. Each call has its own timeout (200 ms, 500 ms for optional ones) and its own pool. Reviews outage leads to an empty reviews section. Recommendations fall back to a cached bestseller list. Checkout is unaffected because it runs in its own service group.

## Interview tip
Name the failure, name the degraded behaviour, and say how you would detect and recover automatically. Classify features as critical or optional ahead of time.
keyPoints: Decide in advance which features are critical and which can degrade: defaults, stale cache, disabled features, read-only mode, deferred writes.
Fallback paths are rarely exercised, so test them or prefer simple fail-fast designs.
Bulkheads isolate pools, instances or cells per dependency, tenant or criticality so one failure cannot exhaust shared resources.
Shuffle sharding and cells bound the blast radius of a bad tenant or deploy.

## Definitions
- RPO (recovery point objective): how much data you can afford to lose, measured as time. RPO of 5 minutes means you must be able to restore to a state at most 5 minutes old.
- RTO (recovery time objective): how long the service can be down before you must be back. RTO of 1 hour means recovery must complete within an hour.
Both are business decisions. Tighter targets cost more. Ask: what does an hour of downtime cost?

## Backups
- Types: full, incremental (changes since the last backup), differential. Continuous archiving of the write-ahead log supports point-in-time recovery (PITR), letting you restore to just before a bad delete.
- Follow the 3-2-1 rule: 3 copies, 2 media types, 1 offsite (different region or account).
- Protect against ransomware and operator error: immutable (write-once) backups, separate credentials and account, and delete protection.
- A backup that has never been restored is not a backup. Test restores regularly and measure the restore time, because it determines the real RTO. Restoring multi-TB can take hours.
- Backups guard against corruption and human error. Replication does not: a bad delete replicates instantly.

## DR strategies (AWS names, increasing cost and decreasing RTO and RPO)
- Backup and restore: RPO hours, RTO hours or more. Cheapest.
- Pilot light: core data replicated continuously, minimal servers off or tiny. Scale up on disaster. RTO tens of minutes to hours.
- Warm standby: a scaled-down but running copy of the full stack. RTO minutes.
- Multi-site active-active: full capacity in several regions. RTO near zero, RPO near zero or small, highest cost and complexity.

## Failover
- Detect: health checks from outside the failing region, with enough evidence to avoid false triggers (flapping).
- Decide: automatic for fast RTO, or human-approved for risky actions such as promoting a database, where false failover and split brain are costly.
- Promote the replica, redirect traffic (DNS with low TTL, global load balancer, anycast), warm caches, and scale up capacity.
- Avoid split brain with fencing: ensure the old primary can no longer accept writes.
- Failback: return to the primary after repair, often as hard as failover. Plan it.
- Asynchronous replication means the replica lags, so promotion can lose the tail of writes (RPO above zero). Synchronous replication reduces data loss at the cost of write latency.
- Dependencies: DNS, identity provider, secrets, CI/CD, and third-party services must also survive. Many DR plans fail because of a forgotten dependency, or because the control plane is in the failed region.

## Practice
Runbooks, regular DR drills in production-like environments, infrastructure as code to rebuild quickly, and documented ownership. Keep capacity quotas in the DR region.

## Example
Order database, RPO 1 minute, RTO 15 minutes. Use cross-region async replica (lag under seconds) plus PITR backups. Warm standby app tier at 30 percent capacity with autoscaling. Runbook: promote replica, flip traffic, scale up. Quarterly drill measuring the actual figures.
keyPoints: RPO is acceptable data loss; RTO is acceptable downtime; both are business decisions that drive cost.
Backups protect against corruption and human error (replication does not); test restores and keep immutable offsite copies.
DR options in order of cost: backup and restore, pilot light, warm standby, multi-site active-active.
Failover needs detection, fencing against split brain, traffic redirection, and a tested failback; drill regularly.

## What it is
Chaos engineering is the discipline of experimenting on a system in production-like conditions to build confidence in its ability to withstand turbulent conditions. It started at Netflix (Chaos Monkey, which terminates random instances) and is codified in the Principles of Chaos Engineering.

It is not random breakage. It is the scientific method applied to reliability.

## The experiment loop
1. Define steady state with a measurable business or SLI metric (orders per minute, stream starts per second, p99 latency). Not CPU.
2. Hypothesise: "if one availability zone's cache goes down, steady state holds, with latency up by less than 20 percent."
3. Inject realistic failures: kill instances or pods, add network latency or packet loss, block a dependency, exhaust disk or CPU, fail a zone, expire certificates, skew clocks, throttle a database.
4. Observe and compare against the control group or baseline.
5. Fix the weaknesses found, then repeat and automate.

## Safety rules
- Start small with a limited blast radius: one instance, a small percentage of traffic, one non-critical service, staging first, then production.
- Have an abort condition and a kill switch: stop automatically if the SLI drops below a threshold.
- Run in business hours with the team watching, and notify stakeholders.
- Ensure observability is good before starting, or you cannot learn anything.
- Do not run chaos on a system known to be broken. Fix the known problem first.

## Game days
A scheduled exercise where the team rehearses a failure scenario together, such as "primary database fails" or "region evacuated".
- Participants play their roles on-call, using real runbooks, dashboards and communication channels. A facilitator injects the failure, and scribes record the timeline.
- Goals: validate runbooks, alerts and dashboards, find gaps in knowledge and access (can on-call actually promote the replica?), train new people, and measure real detection and recovery times against RTO and RPO.
- Follow with a blameless review and tracked action items.
Types: tabletop (talk through), staging, and production game days.

## Tools
Chaos Monkey, Gremlin, AWS Fault Injection Service, Chaos Mesh and Litmus for Kubernetes, Toxiproxy for network faults.

## What it finds
Missing timeouts, retry storms, a fallback that does not work, hidden single points of failure, alerts that never fire, autoscaling that is too slow, stale runbooks, and cross-service coupling.

## Interview tips
Connect it to the other reliability patterns: chaos experiments verify that your timeouts, circuit breakers, bulkheads and failover really work. State the steady-state metric, hypothesis, blast radius and abort criteria. It complements, not replaces, testing and load tests.
keyPoints: Chaos engineering tests hypotheses about steady state (a business or SLI metric) by injecting real failures, not random breakage.
Limit blast radius, define abort conditions, and ensure observability before running experiments, ideally in production gradually.
Game days rehearse incident scenarios with real runbooks to validate alerts, access, procedures and recovery time versus RTO and RPO.
It verifies resilience patterns such as timeouts, breakers, bulkheads and failover actually work; follow with blameless reviews.
